In the triangle above, what is the length of the shorter leg?
question.worked_solution:
Let's refer to our standard ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14233096/assets/75e75d1190cda98916cc6071cb2c0c2d25985fabafeda774cfafa5d3e60a7cb8.png)

Since this is a ${30}^{∘}$-${60}^{∘}$-${90}^{∘}$ triangle, the length of the longer leg is $\sqrt{3}$ times that of the shorter leg.

Here, the longer leg has length $3,$ and the shorter leg has length $x,$ so we have

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =\sqrt{3}x \\ x & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

To remove the radical from the denominator, we can multiply the numerator and denominator by the radical:

$$
x=\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}}=\frac{3\cdot \sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{3}}=\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{3}=\sqrt{3}
$$

So, the length of the shorter leg is $\sqrt{3}.$
